text: he dropped his ears and wagged his tail
author: Homer
location: Book 17, Argos recognises the arriving Odysseus
speaker: Narrator
context: A physical sign of recognition despite the master's disguise.
fit: A tender bodily action, more specific than a generic quotation about loyalty.

text: Tell me, O muse
author: Homer
location: Book 1, opening invocation
speaker: Narrator
context: The singer invokes divine assistance to tell the journey.
fit: Short opening phrase fits the selection spell without pretending to be rules text.

text: you have thundered from a clear sky
author: Homer
location: Book 20, Zeus's confirming thunder
speaker: Odysseus
context: Odysseus asks for a sign and recognizes thunder under a clear sky as confirmation.
fit: The impossible weather sign is the card's exact subject and remains short enough for a common.

text: I will find you a ship, and will come with you myself.
location: Book 2, Athena in Mentor's likeness prepares Telemachus's voyage
speaker: Athena in Mentor's likeness
context: Athena, appearing as Mentor, promises to secure the ship and accompany Telemachus.
fit: The line makes Mentor's practical counsel and voyage-readiness concrete.
author: Homer

text: I may drink of the blood and answer your questions truly.
location: Book 11, Tiresias at the blood trench
speaker: Tiresias
context: Tiresias asks to drink from the trench so he can speak truthfully to Odysseus.
fit: It joins graveyard ritual to the knowledge Tiresias supplies.
author: Homer

text: All deaths are bad enough but there is none so bad as famine.
location: Book 12, Eurylochus argues for killing Helios's cattle
speaker: Eurylochus
context: Hunger drives Eurylochus to argue for the forbidden slaughter.
fit: The line captures the desperate reasoning behind sacrificing long-term safety for immediate survival.
author: Homer

text: Eat, my good fellow, and enjoy your supper, such as it is.
location: Book 14, Eumaeus feeds the disguised Odysseus
speaker: Eumaeus
context: Eumaeus offers the stranger what food he has before knowing his identity.
fit: Directly expresses Eumaeus's hospitality and Food-centered design.
author: Homer

text: you are more fond of eating things yourself than of giving them to other people.
location: Book 17, Telemachus rebukes Antinous
speaker: Telemachus
context: Telemachus condemns Antinous for consuming rather than sharing the household's resources.
fit: A sharp source-text statement of the consumption engine.
author: Homer

text: Thrice I sprang towards her and tried to clasp her in my arms
location: Book 11, Odysseus tries to embrace Anticleia
speaker: Odysseus
context: Odysseus repeatedly tries and fails to embrace his mother's shade.
fit: The failed embrace makes Anticleia's graveyard/return identity emotionally specific.
author: Homer

text: trust in Jove and row on with might and main.
location: Book 12, Odysseus commands the crew
speaker: Odysseus
context: Odysseus rallies the crew to keep rowing through danger.
fit: The ordinary Deck-Captain is composite, but this line cleanly represents coordinated rowing under command.
author: Homer

text: do not forget me when you are safe at home again
location: Book 8, Nausicaa asks to be remembered
speaker: Nausicaa
context: As Odysseus prepares to leave Scheria, Nausicaa asks that he remember the one who helped him.
fit: A concise expression of recognition, care, and successful onward return.
author: Homer

text: I will point out to you the trees in the vineyard which you gave me
location: Book 24, Odysseus proves himself to Laertes
speaker: Odysseus
context: Odysseus recalls the trees Laertes gave him as a child to prove their shared history.
fit: The remembered trees are the most specific source hook for Laertes's rooted recovery identity.
author: Homer

text: this is no dream, but a vision of good omen
author: Homer
location: Book 19, the eagle interprets Penelope's dream
speaker: Eagle in Penelope's dream
context: The eagle declares the geese dream a true omen of Odysseus's return and the suitors' destruction.
fit: Directly names the dream as an omen while preserving Penelope's surrounding uncertainty.

text: the sun is blotted out of heaven
author: Homer
location: Book 20, Theoclymenus's vision
speaker: Theoclymenus
context: The prophet sees blood, ghosts and darkness over the hall and announces the suitors' doom.
fit: A compact image from the exact vision gives the black Omen dread without explaining the whole prophecy.

text: the joints upon the spits began to low like cows
author: Homer
location: Book 12, omen after Helios's cattle are slaughtered
speaker: Narrator
context: After the crew violates the taboo, the hides crawl and the roasting meat bellows before punishment follows.
fit: The uncanny physical sign is the card's exact image and carries the horror of the violated oath.

text: there will be no house in Ithaca more royal than your own
author: Homer
location: Book 15, Theoclymenus interprets the hawk
speaker: Theoclymenus
context: A hawk carrying a dove crosses on the right and is read as a sign of the enduring rule of Odysseus's house.
fit: It states the interpretation of the bird omen rather than merely describing the animal.

text: the man is guiltless, do him no hurt
location: Book 22, Telemachus defends Medon
speaker: Telemachus
context: Telemachus intervenes so the innocent herald Medon is spared.
fit: The line exactly captures Medon's survival amid the household deaths.
author: Homer

text: change your song and tell us of the wooden horse
location: Book 8, Odysseus requests Demodocus's Trojan Horse song
speaker: Odysseus
context: Odysseus asks Demodocus to sing the story of the wooden horse.
fit: It makes the card's status as an actual performed song explicit.
author: Homer

text: I will bring you arms from the store room
location: Book 22, Melanthius arms the suitors
speaker: Melanthius
context: Melanthius volunteers to fetch weapons for the suitors during the hall battle.
fit: A direct statement of his active betrayal and resource conversion.
author: Homer

text: he could stir or still each one of them according to his own pleasure
location: Book 10, Aeolus controls the winds
speaker: Narrator
context: Aeolus is described as able to rouse or quiet the winds at will.
fit: The line maps directly onto his Vehicle acceleration and wind-bottling Adventure.
author: Homer

text: let us call her and see whether she is woman or goddess.
location: Book 10, Polites urges the crew toward Circe's house
speaker: Polites
context: Polites persuades the scouting party to call to the singer inside Circe's house.
fit: It captures the decisive first-through-the-door impulse behind the card.
author: Homer

text: at night I would unpick the stitches
author: Homer
location: Book 19, Penelope recounts the shroud deception
speaker: Penelope
context: She explains to the disguised Odysseus how she postponed the marriage.
fit: The action is exactly the rare proposal's unweaving hook.

text: when they had drunk she turned them into pigs by a stroke of her wand
location: Book 10, Circe transforms the crew
speaker: Narrator
context: Circe drugs and transforms Odysseus's companions.
fit: The exact transformation scene grounds the face-down/enchantment-death identity.
author: Homer

text: you would stay where you are, keep house along with me
location: Book 5, Calypso urges Odysseus to remain
speaker: Calypso
context: Calypso offers continued life with her on Ogygia instead of departure.
fit: The line directly expresses comfort becoming captivity and delayed homecoming.
author: Homer

text: Father, I have always heard of your renown both in the field and in council
location: Book 16, Telemachus recognises Odysseus
speaker: Telemachus
context: After the reunion, Telemachus addresses the father whose reputation he has inherited.
fit: It bridges returned son, inherited identity, and the coming coordinated fight.
author: Homer

text: if anything has been said amiss may the winds blow it away with them
location: Book 8, Euryalus apologises to Odysseus
speaker: Euryalus
context: After insulting Odysseus and seeing his athletic prowess, Euryalus apologises and offers a gift.
fit: It completes Euryalus's sequence from challenge to recognition and reconciliation.
author: Homer

text: To strive, to seek, to find, and not to yield.
author: Alfred, Lord Tennyson
location: Final line
speaker: Tennyson's Ulysses
context: The later poem ends with resolve to continue voyaging.
fit: Matches the deliberately restless reception version rather than Homeric homecoming.

text: So I’ll spin my own thread.
author: Margaret Atwood
location: Excerpt on author's book page; edition pagination not verified
speaker: Penelope
context: Penelope claims the right to tell her own story.
fit: Directly fits the Teller of Her Own Tale version.
